8.title: 2011 Super Outbreak
8.content:
2011 Super Outbreak[![Image 1: Satellite view of a large cloud formation stretching from the Midwest to the southeastern United States](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Apr_27_2011_tornado_outbreak_Southern_USA.jpg/330px-Apr_27_2011_tornado_outbreak_Southern_USA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apr_27_2011_tornado_outbreak_Southern_USA.jpg)

[![Image 2: Doppler weather radar displaying a supercell thunderstorm with high reflectivity and velocity signatures](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Radar_image_of_the_2011_Tuscaloosa_tornado_April_27%2C_2011_2210Z.png/250px-Radar_image_of_the_2011_Tuscaloosa_tornado_April_27%2C_2011_2210Z.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radar_image_of_the_2011_Tuscaloosa_tornado_April_27,_2011_2210Z.png)

[![Image 3: An abandoned building and debris from a tornado](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Damage%2C_from_Tuscaloosa-Birmingham%2C_Alabama_tornado%2C_%28viewed_by_Secretary_Shaun_Donovan_during_visit_to_the_state%29_-_DPLA_-_543b63cbbb54dab5e37a2b3dbb61a0a0.jpg/250px-Damage%2C_from_Tuscaloosa-Birmingham%2C_Alabama_tornado%2C_%28viewed_by_Secretary_Shaun_Donovan_during_visit_to_the_state%29_-_DPLA_-_543b63cbbb54dab5e37a2b3dbb61a0a0.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Damage,_from_Tuscaloosa-Birmingham,_Alabama_tornado,_(viewed_by_Secretary_Shaun_Donovan_during_visit_to_the_state)_-_DPLA_-_543b63cbbb54dab5e37a2b3dbb61a0a0.jpg)

[![Image 4: Aerial view of a town devastated by a tornado, with trees uprooted and buildings damaged](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_Tornado_Damage_%28NWS%29.jpg/250px-2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_Tornado_Damage_%28NWS%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_Tornado_Damage_(NWS).jpg)

[![Image 5: Flags on a pole over a collapsed building and a large field with tree stumps in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Smithville%2C_MS_post_office_damage.jpg/250px-Smithville%2C_MS_post_office_damage.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithville,_MS_post_office_damage.jpg)

**Clockwise from top:** The storm system responsible for the outbreak on April 27, heavy damage to buildings in [Tuscaloosa, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscaloosa,_Alabama "Tuscaloosa, Alabama") after [an EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tuscaloosa_tornado "2011 Tuscaloosa tornado"), flags raised above a post office in [Smithville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithville,_Mississippi "Smithville, Mississippi") after [an EF5 tornado hit the town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Smithville_tornado "2011 Smithville tornado"), an aerial view of EF5-rated tornado damage in [Hackleburg, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama "Hackleburg, Alabama") after [a violent tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Hackleburg_tornado "2011 Hackleburg tornado") moved through the town, a visible [hook echo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_echo "Hook echo") that would produce a violent tornado in Tuscaloosa
Meteorological history
Duration April 25–28, 2011
Tornado outbreak
Tornadoes[368 confirmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_in_the_2011_Super_Outbreak "List of tornadoes in the 2011 Super Outbreak")

(Record for a continuous outbreak)
Maximum rating[EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")
Duration 3 days, 7 hours, 18 minutes
Highest winds**Tornadic** – 210 mph (340 km/h) ([Hackleburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama "Hackleburg, Alabama")–[Phil Campbell, AL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell,_Alabama "Phil Campbell, Alabama") EF5 on April 27)
Highest gusts**Non-tornadic** – 113 mph (182 km/h) (near [Bay, AR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay,_Arkansas "Bay, Arkansas") on April 27)
Largest hail 4.5 in (11 cm) in [Saltville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltville,_Virginia "Saltville, Virginia") on April 27
[Extratropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone")
Lowest pressure 990 [hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)") ([mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")); 29.23[inHg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch_of_mercury "Inch of mercury")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-1)
Maximum rainfall 19.26 in (48.9 cm) in [Springdale, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springdale,_Arkansas "Springdale, Arkansas")
Maximum snowfall or ice accretion 6 inches (15 cm) in [Bayfield County, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayfield_County,_Wisconsin "Bayfield County, Wisconsin")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2)
Overall effects
Fatalities 324 (+24 non-tornadic)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-spc_fatal-3)
Injuries 3,100+[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-cbs342-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Vilonia-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-cnn-6)
Damage$10.2 billion (2011 [USD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD"))

$14.26 billion (2024 USD)

(Second-costliest tornado outbreak on record; costliest on record when accounting for [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation"))[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-7)
Areas affected[Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"), [Midwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States"), &[Eastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_United_States "Eastern United States")
* * *

Part of the **[tornado outbreaks of 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_of_2011 "Tornadoes of 2011")**

The **2011 Super Outbreak** was the largest and costliest[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Inflation-9)[tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") ever recorded, taking place in the [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"), [Midwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwest "Midwest"), and [Northeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States")[United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") from April 25 to 28, 2011, leaving catastrophic destruction in its wake.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-noaanews-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-13) Over 175 tornadoes struck [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), and [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), which were the most severely damaged states. Other destructive tornadoes occurred in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), and [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), with storms also affecting other states in the Southern and Eastern United States. In total, 368 tornadoes were confirmed by [NOAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")'s [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") (NWS) and [Government of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada")'s [Environment Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_Canada "Environment Canada") in 21 states from [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") to [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State "New York State") to southern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). Widespread and destructive tornadoes occurred on each day of the outbreak. April 27 was the most active day, with a record 224 tornadoes touching down that day from midnight to midnight [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (05:00–05:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")). Four of the tornadoes were rated EF5, which is the highest ranking on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale"); typically these tornadoes are recorded no more than once a year.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-noaanews-12)

In total, 348 people were killed as a result of the outbreak, including 324 tornado-related deaths across six states and 24 fatalities caused by other [thunderstorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm")-related events such as [straight-line winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downbursts "Downbursts"), [hail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail "Hail"), [flash flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_flooding "Flash flooding") or [lightning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning "Lightning").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-alemapressrelease1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-tuscaloosa_missing-15) In Alabama alone, 238 tornado-related deaths were confirmed by the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) and the state's [Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_management "Emergency management").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-spc_fatal-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-alemapressrelease1-14) April 27's 316 fatalities were the most tornado-related fatalities in the United States in a single day since the "[Tri-State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tri-State_tornado_outbreak "Tri-State tornado outbreak")" outbreak on March 18, 1925 (when at least 751 people were killed).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-cnn1925outbreak-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-cbsSouth-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-second_deadliest-19) Nearly 500 preliminary [local storm reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_storm_report "Local storm report") were received for tornadoes over four days, including 292 in 16 states on April 27 alone.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Reports_April_27-20) This event was the costliest tornado outbreak in United States history, with total damage reaching $10.2 billion (equivalent to $14 billion in 2024).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NCEIbillion-21) In 2023, tornado expert [Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") created the [outbreak intensity score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outbreak_intensity_score "Outbreak intensity score") (OIS) as a way to rank various tornado outbreaks. The 2011 Super Outbreak received an OIS of 383, making it the second most intense tornado outbreak in recorded history behind only the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-22)

The outbreak was caused by a vigorous upper-level [trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trough_(meteorology) "Trough (meteorology)") that moved into the Southern Plains states on April 25. An [extratropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone") developed ahead of this upper-level trough between northeastern [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") and western [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), and moved northeastward.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-SS11-23) Conditions were similar on April 26, with a predicted likelihood of [severe thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_thunderstorm "Severe thunderstorm"), including an extended threat of strong to violent long-track tornadoes throughout the afternoon and evening; mixed-layer [CAPE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_available_potential_energy "Convective available potential energy") values were forecast to be around 3000–4000 J/kg, around east [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), and [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"). The storm mode on April 26 was predicted to include mostly discrete tornadic [supercells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") during both the afternoon and the early evening, shifting over to a [mesoscale convective complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_convective_complex "Mesoscale convective complex"), with more of a threat of damaging winds and hail during the nighttime.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-24)

As the storm system moved eastward toward the Ohio, Mississippi, and Tennessee Valleys on April 27, a very powerful 80–100 [knot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_(unit) "Knot (unit)") mid-level [jet stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream "Jet stream") moved into the [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley") and [Tennessee Valleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley "Tennessee Valley") behind the trough and created strong [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear"), along with a low pressure center moving quickly northeastward across those areas on April 27. During the afternoon of April 27, CAPE values were estimated to be in the range of 2000–3000 J/kg across Louisiana and southern Mississippi, with the moderate instability moving northeastward across the southern Tennessee Valley; additionally, temperatures across the southeastern United States ranged from the 70s°F (mid-20s°C) to the lower 90s°F (near 35°C). [Helicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrodynamical_helicity "Hydrodynamical helicity") levels ranged from 450 to 600 m 2/s 2, which supported some significant tornadic activity and strong to violent long-track tornadoes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April27-25)

A total of 56 severe weather watches were issued by the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) over those four days in the outbreak area. This included 41 [tornado watches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch")—10 of which were [particularly dangerous situation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation") (PDS) watches—and 15 [severe thunderstorm watches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_thunderstorm_watch "Severe thunderstorm watch").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-27) The SPC assigns numbers to each severe weather watch issued starting at the beginning of each year; the organization unsuccessfully used two of their allocated watch numbers during this outbreak (numbers 208 and 209).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-review-28)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

A large area of possible severe storms for April 25–27 was forecast as the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) issued a moderate risk of severe weather for three consecutive days, centered over Arkansas through Tennessee. At 3:25 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (20:25 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")), the SPC issued a [particularly dangerous situation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation") (PDS) [tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch") for much of Arkansas and parts of Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, and [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Apr25SPC-29) By the evening of April 25, tornadoes had been reported across a few states, some of which caused significant damage in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"). An intense [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") thunderstorm tracked near the [Little Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock,_Arkansas "Little Rock, Arkansas") area and a [tornado emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") was declared for the city of [Vilonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilonia,_Arkansas "Vilonia, Arkansas"). A large [EF2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")[wedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedge_tornado "Wedge tornado") tornado struck the town, subsequently causing severe damage and killing four people.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-MSNBC_Arkansas-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-New_York_Times_AR_Tornado-31) A strong EF3 tornado also struck the [Hot Springs Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs_Village,_Arkansas "Hot Springs Village, Arkansas") area earlier that evening; the tornado caused severe damage and resulted in one death. Later that evening, another EF2 tornado caused extensive damage to both a school building and [Little Rock Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock_Air_Force_Base "Little Rock Air Force Base") as well.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-32) Severe [flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood "Flood") continued across a large area from the [Red River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_South "Red River of the South") valley to the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-33) A total of 42 tornadoes and five tornado-related deaths were confirmed on the 25th.

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Severe_Tornado_Outbreak_in_the_Southern_United_States.ogv "Play video")[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Severe_Tornado_Outbreak_in_the_Southern_United_States.ogv)

This animation of satellite images from April 26 through the morning of April 28 shows the development of the storm system which spawned the tornadoes.

A [high risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_SPC_high-risk_days "List of SPC high-risk days") of severe weather was issued for April 26 for portions of Louisiana, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas along and near the [Interstate 30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_30 "Interstate 30") corridor as conditions became even more favorable for extreme weather.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-HighRisk0426-34) A large PDS tornado watch with very high possibilities for tornadoes was issued for that same area that afternoon.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-35) Widespread [tornado warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") were then issued in that area later that evening.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-38)

An upper-level negatively tilted trough with two embedded shortwaves generated two surface lows that propagated generally east. One of the surface lows tracked northeast along the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") into [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin") as it occluded. Tornado watches were issued for the Lower Great Lakes during the afternoon as supercell thunderstorms developed along the warm front lifting north across central [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan"). Two tornadoes touched down in Michigan and caused damage to farm structures. Further east, severe thunderstorms caused scattered wind damage and large hail across Pennsylvania and New York. Two-inch-diameter hail was reported in [Lock Haven, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lock_Haven,_Pennsylvania "Lock Haven, Pennsylvania").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Reports_April_26-39) An isolated supercell moved across Central New York throughout much of the afternoon, producing golf ball-sized hail in [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_New_York "Syracuse, New York") and spawning a very brief EF1 tornado in [Verona Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verona_Mills,_New_York "Verona Mills, New York"), which primarily caused damage to trees. Another tornado – this one being in [Gilbertsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbertsville,_New_York "Gilbertsville, New York") – caused significant damage to a school's athletic field.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-40)

The second surface low corresponded to an area of strong upper level divergence ahead of the downstream shortwave. As the low formed across Texas and deepened while moving east, a tightening pressure gradient force further strengthened the low-level jet, therefore creating a broad warm sector across the southeastern states. This also generated stronger wind shear, providing better organization for the supercell storms as a result. Numerous tornadoes touched down across several states, including Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas. Most of those tornadoes were weak, but a few of them caused considerable damage. A long-tracked wedge tornado caused EF2 damage in rural portions of Texas and Louisiana.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Shreveport-042611-41) An EF3 tornado destroyed structures and caused severe damage at [Fort Campbell, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Campbell,_Kentucky "Fort Campbell, Kentucky"), as well.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-42) A total of 55 tornadoes were confirmed on the 26th, although no fatalities occurred.

Overnight severe weather persisted into the early morning hours of April 27, and would continue virtually unbroken for the remainder of the day. At 06:10 UTC, the SPC issued a second-consecutive, high risk day-one outlook, featuring a 30% hatched risk of tornadoes centered over northern Alabama.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-43) At 16:30 UTC (11:30 AM CDT) this region was expanded to include portions of eastern Mississippi, southern Tennessee, and northwest Georgia. Additionally, an exceedingly rare, 45% hatched risk of tornadoes was introduced along a corridor from [Meridian, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi"), to [Huntsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama"). Environmental conditions continued to be extremely favorable for discrete tornadic supercells throughout the day.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April27-25)

#### Morning squall lines

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Morning squall lines")]

During the early morning, a cold front with several embedded low pressure areas extended from east [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") northeastward into the [Ohio River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River_Valley "Ohio River Valley"). An upper-level disturbance that had moved across the frontal boundary the previous evening sparked an area of thunderstorms that morphed into a [squall line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall_line "Squall line"). This line of severe thunderstorms would produce tornadic activity from the evening on April 26 into the late morning of April 27. Early in the morning the squall line, packing straight-line winds and numerous embedded tornadoes, moved through [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") and [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi") before proceeding to affect [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Alabama "North Alabama") and [Central Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Alabama "Central Alabama") and parts of [Middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Tennessee "Middle Tennessee") and [East Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Tennessee "East Tennessee"). The line strengthened as it moved through [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), partially due to a high amount of low-level moisture from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") and increasing [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

A majority of the tornadoes embedded in this initial squall line were weak, though several were strong and as such caused significant damage. An EF3 tornado caused major damage to homes in [Coaling, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaling,_Alabama "Coaling, Alabama"), an EF2 and an EF3 tornado produced severe damage and a fatality near [Eupora, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eupora,_Mississippi "Eupora, Mississippi"). Another EF3 tornado resulted in heavy damage in downtown [Cordova, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordova,_Alabama "Cordova, Alabama"), which was struck by a violent EF4 tornado later that afternoon. An EF2 also struck [Cahaba Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahaba_Heights "Cahaba Heights") near [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). One embedded cell began producing tornadoes just after 5:00 a.m. CDT (10:00 UTC), starting with an EF1 tornado striking [Berry, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry,_Alabama "Berry, Alabama"). This was soon followed by the Cordova EF3 tornado.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2011-super-outbreak-45) As the line entered [Cullman County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullman_County,_Alabama "Cullman County, Alabama"), the cell, a [mesoscale convective vortex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_convective_vortex "Mesoscale convective vortex") (MCV), began exhibiting a comma head appearance and produced another long-tracked EF2 tornado that struck the town of [Hanceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanceville,_Alabama "Hanceville, Alabama"), killing one person. The MCV would then produce 13 tornadoes (most rated EF1) to the northeast in [Marshall County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_County,_Alabama "Marshall County, Alabama"), many of which occurred simultaneously. Two more tornadoes were produced as the comma head-shaped embedded cell continued northeast along the [Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Alabama "Jackson County, Alabama")/[DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Alabama "DeKalb County, Alabama") county line, including a long-track EF1 that resulted in a fatality near [Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama "Pisgah, Alabama"). The same area was impacted later that day by a [high-end EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#Pisgah%E2%80%93Flat_Rock%E2%80%93Higdon,_Alabama/Trenton,_Georgia).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44) Another EF1 tornado occurred in [Dade County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_County,_Georgia "Dade County, Georgia"), with the cell, and six more tornadoes struck [Hamilton County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_County,_Tennessee "Hamilton County, Tennessee"), five of which were in the [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee") area. The 26th and final tornado produced by the MCV was an EF2 tornado in northern [Bradley County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_County,_Tennessee "Bradley County, Tennessee"), which hit at 9:45 a.m. EDT (13:45 UTC).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-MRXApril27-46) The initial storms caused widespread [power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_line "Power line") and [telephone line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone_line "Telephone line") outages across Alabama and Tennessee. This line of storms also caused some [NOAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")[weather radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Weather_Radio "NOAA Weather Radio") transmitter sites to stop functioning for the remainder of the outbreak. Because of this, more than one million customers were without power and had no warning of any approaching tornadoes later that day.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

From the late morning to the early afternoon, another squall line moved through northern parts of Mississippi and Alabama as high wind shear and low-level moisture persisted. However, this time several discrete [supercells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") developed along and in front of the line, spawning seven weak tornadoes across [Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_County,_Alabama "Morgan County, Alabama"), [Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone_County,_Alabama "Limestone County, Alabama"), and [Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Alabama "Madison County, Alabama") Counties in northern Alabama around noon that day.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

#### Afternoon supercells

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Afternoon supercells")]

[![Image 371: Brown dirt area and a green field are seen under a clear blue sky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Philadelphia%2C_MS_ground_scouring.jpg/250px-Philadelphia%2C_MS_ground_scouring.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philadelphia,_MS_ground_scouring.jpg)

Extremely deep ground scouring near [Philadelphia, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Mississippi "Philadelphia, Mississippi"), caused by a fast-moving EF5 tornado that killed three people.

The most intense supercells of the outbreak developed around midday in central Mississippi and began tracking eastward. With the extreme instability and wind shear, they quickly intensified and eventually became tornadic, shortly thereafter resulting in strong to violent tornadoes. Responding to the high risk issued by the SPC and the already unstable atmosphere expected to become even more unstable throughout the afternoon, a [PDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation")[tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch") was issued at 1:45 p.m. CDT (18:45 UTC) for much of Alabama and portions of Mississippi, Tennessee, and Georgia. A widespread complex of supercell storms overspread the states of Mississippi and Alabama and violent tornadoes began rapidly touching down as the afternoon progressed.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

By mid-afternoon, as wind shear and low-level moisture continued to dramatically increase, a [tornado emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") was declared for [Neshoba County, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neshoba_County,_Mississippi "Neshoba County, Mississippi"), as a large tornado was reported on the ground by both storm spotters and a camera atop a television tower from [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WTOK-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WTOK-TV "WTOK-TV") (channel 11) in [Meridian, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi"). This powerful EF5 tornado caused incredible damage northeast of [Philadelphia, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Mississippi "Philadelphia, Mississippi"), where pavement was torn off from roads, vehicles were thrown, and the ground was scoured out to a depth of 2 feet (0.61 m) by the tornado. Three people died when a mobile home was thrown 300 yards (270 m) into a wooded area, obliterating it in the process.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-47) Another very long-tracked EF4 tornado passed near the town of [Enterprise, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterprise,_Clarke_County,_Mississippi "Enterprise, Clarke County, Mississippi"), killing seven people before crossing into Alabama and eventually dissipating. Four tornadoes were officially rated EF5 on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale") that day. One of those EF5 tornadoes struck the town of [Smithville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithville,_Mississippi "Smithville, Mississippi"), where many well-built brick homes were reduced to bare slabs, numerous hardwood trees were completely debarked, and an SUV was hurled half a mile into the top of the town's water tower, subsequently leaving behind a visible dent. Another long-tracked EF5 wedge tornado passed through rural portions of Alabama and Tennessee, becoming the deadliest tornado of the outbreak as it completely devastated the towns of [Hackleburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama "Hackleburg, Alabama"), [Phil Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell,_Alabama "Phil Campbell, Alabama"), [Mount Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Hope,_Lawrence_County,_Alabama "Mount Hope, Lawrence County, Alabama"), [Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner,_Alabama "Tanner, Alabama"), and [Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest,_Alabama "Harvest, Alabama"), killing 72 people. This marks only the second day in history (after [April 3, 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak")) that there were more than two F5/EF5 tornadoes reported.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-48)

The tornadoes continued tracking through central Alabama that afternoon and into the early evening. A dangerous and destructive tornado struck the city of [Cullman, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullman,_Alabama "Cullman, Alabama"), at around 3:00 p.m. CDT (20:00 UTC). This large, multiple-vortex tornado was captured on several tower cameras from [television stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_station "Television station"), such as [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WBRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBRC "WBRC") (channel 6) and ABC affiliate [WBMA-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBMA-LD "WBMA-LD")/[WCFT-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSES "WSES")/[WJSU-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGWW "WGWW") (channels 58, 33, and 40) both out of [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). The tornado caused extensive destruction in the city's downtown area; it was ultimately rated EF4. The final damage count was 867 residences and 94 businesses in Cullman; six people died as well.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27,_2011,_Cullman,_Alabama_EF4_Tornado-49) The town of [Cordova, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordova,_Alabama "Cordova, Alabama"), which had already been damaged by an EF3 tornado from the initial round of storms, was struck by an EF4 tornado that killed 13 people. Two violent EF4 tornadoes also ripped through [Jackson County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Alabama "Jackson County, Alabama"), one of which caused a fatality near [Bridgeport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgeport,_Alabama "Bridgeport, Alabama") while the other passed near [Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama "Pisgah, Alabama") and into Georgia where it caused major damage in [Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton,_Georgia "Trenton, Georgia") and killed 14 people. At around 5:10 p.m. CDT (22:10 UTC), a very large and exceptionally destructive tornado struck [Tuscaloosa, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscaloosa,_Alabama "Tuscaloosa, Alabama"), and about 40 minutes later, that same tornado struck the northern suburbs of nearby Birmingham.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-massive-50) A tornado emergency was issued for both cities, along with many other cities that day. Many local television stations, including WBRC and WBMA-LD/WCFT/WJSU, as well as [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") affiliate [WIAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIAT "WIAT") (channel 42), broadcast live footage of this long-tracked tornado in both Tuscaloosa and Birmingham. A debris ball was observed by the Birmingham [NEXRAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEXRAD "NEXRAD"), indicating that the tornado was causing extreme damage.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-51) This tornado killed 64 people and caused extensive devastation in densely populated areas, and the tornado struck several of the same small communities as the [April 1956 F4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1956_Birmingham_tornado "April 1956 Birmingham tornado"), the [April 1977 F5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1977_Birmingham_tornado "April 1977 Birmingham tornado") and the [April 1998 F5 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Oak_Grove%E2%80%93Birmingham_tornado "1998 Oak Grove–Birmingham tornado") that hit portions of the Birmingham area. The supercell that produced the Tuscaloosa/Birmingham EF4 tornado originated in [Newton County, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_County,_Mississippi "Newton County, Mississippi"). The same supercell produced another EF4 tornado later that evening that killed 22 people and struck the [Ohatchee, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohatchee,_Alabama "Ohatchee, Alabama"), area and eventually crossed into Georgia, causing additional damage near [Cave Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_Spring,_Georgia "Cave Spring, Georgia") before dissipating. Further to the south, a mile-wide EF3 tornado killed 7 people in mostly rural areas and caused major damage in the small town of [Eoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"). The final EF5 tornado of the day caused remarkable damage in and around the town of [Rainsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainsville,_Alabama "Rainsville, Alabama"), killing 25 people before crossing into Georgia and dissipating. Tornadoes continued touching down further to the northeast as the sun set, particularly in Georgia. This included a long-tracked EF4 tornado that caused major damage in [Ringgold, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringgold,_Georgia "Ringgold, Georgia"), [Apison, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apison,_Tennessee "Apison, Tennessee"), and [Cleveland, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland,_Tennessee "Cleveland, Tennessee"), killing 20 people along the path. After dark, violent tornadoes continued to touch down, and a nighttime EF4 tornado destroyed many lakeside homes at [Lake Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Martin "Lake Martin") in eastern Alabama, killing seven people. Additional strong nighttime tornadoes occurred in Georgia, including an EF3 that killed two people in [Barnesville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnesville,_Georgia "Barnesville, Georgia"), and another EF3 that destroyed homes and killed one person at [Lake Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Burton_(Georgia) "Lake Burton (Georgia)").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2011-super-outbreak-45)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-52)

#### Continued activity farther east

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Continued activity farther east")]

Powerful tornadoes touched down across [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") as well that evening. A violent EF4 struck the community of [New Harmony, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Harmony,_Tennessee "New Harmony, Tennessee"), where homes were leveled, vehicles were tossed, and four people were killed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-53) On January 23, 2025, Anthony W. Lyza with the [National Severe Storms Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "National Severe Storms Laboratory") along with Harold E. Brooks and Makenzie J. Kroca with the [University of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma")'s School of Meteorology published a paper to the [American Meteorological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Meteorological_Society "American Meteorological Society"), where they stated the tornado in New Harmony was an "EF5 candidate". The paper was of the opinion that the EF5 starting wind speed should be 190 mph (310 km/h) instead of 201 mph (323 km/h).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Lyza2025-54)

Two EF3 tornadoes crossed paths in [Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene_County,_Tennessee "Greene County, Tennessee") and [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_County,_Tennessee "Washington County, Tennessee") counties (coming a couple of hours apart), resulting in eight fatalities. The rural communities of [Horse Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_Creek,_Tennessee "Horse Creek, Tennessee") and [Camp Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Creek,_Tennessee "Camp Creek, Tennessee") suffered major damage from those tornadoes late that evening.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-56) A very large EF4 wedge tornado leveled a mile-wide swath of forest through 14 miles (23 km) of [Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains_National_Park "Great Smoky Mountains National Park"), resulting in many trails being closed.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-58) At [Chilhowee Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilhowee_Dam "Chilhowee Dam"), large metal power line truss towers were torn and thrown from their concrete supports that they were anchored to.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-59)

A secondary area of severe weather also developed that afternoon and evening along a corridor extending from central and northern [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") northward through [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), continuing into early April 28. Many tornadoes touched down in this area as well.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-61) Most of these tornadoes were weak, though an EF2 tornado touched down near the town of [Halifax, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Virginia "Halifax, Virginia"), and caused severe damage to homes in the area, resulting in one death.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-62) Tornado alerts were issued for [Southern Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ontario "Southern Ontario") as far north as [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa") as well; one tornado was later confirmed in [Fergus, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fergus,_Ontario "Fergus, Ontario").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-63)

[![Image 372: SPC Storm Reports for 04/27/11 map updated at 12112 on 05/07/11, with tornado, wind, hail and total reports, high wind and large hail reports](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png/250px-SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png)

SPC Storm Reports for April 27

A statewide review by emergency management officials recorded 249 fatalities in Alabama as of the morning of April 30, 23 of which were not tornado-related.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-alemapressrelease1-14) Eventually, a total of 238 tornado-related deaths would be confirmed in the state. Damage and power outages in the [Huntsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama") area were so widespread that at one point over 650,000 people were out of power in the [Tennessee Valley Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley_Authority "Tennessee Valley Authority") system. The EF5 tornado that struck Hackleburg and Phil Campbell damaged main high-transmission power lines coming from [Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browns_Ferry_Nuclear_Plant "Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant") near [Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner,_Alabama "Tanner, Alabama"). These towers were the main supply of electrical power to much of North Alabama, and some were without power for two weeks. The tornado just missed the Limestone Correctional Facility, which less than a year later would be struck by another tornado.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-65)

The Storm Prediction Center received 292 reports of tornadoes in the preceding 24 hours.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Reports_April_27-20) In addition to setting the record for most tornadoes in a calendar day (223; midnight to midnight CDT (05:00 – 05:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time"))), it also broke the record for the most tornado touchdowns in any 24-hour period with 226 from 12:40 a.m. to 12:40 a.m. CDT (05:40 – 05:40 UTC) April 27–28, breaking the old 24-hour record of 148 set by the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak"). Of those 226 tornadoes, 59 touched down in Alabama and 83 began in Tennessee, accounting for 62.8 percent of the tornadoes that touched down on April 27.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-66) On April 27 alone, the National Weather Service in Huntsville, Alabama, issued 92 tornado warnings, 31 [severe thunderstorm warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_thunderstorm_warning "Severe thunderstorm warning"), and seven [flash flood warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_flood_warning "Flash flood warning").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-SWDJW-04272011-WarningSummaries-67)

Tornado watches were issued for the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") coast from [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") at the start of the day and continued through the morning and early afternoon, but tornadoes were forecasted to generally be weaker and more isolated.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-68) Despite this, the secondary portion of the outbreak that had begun producing scattered tornadoes throughout the [Mid-Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_states "Mid-Atlantic states") and [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") regions the previous evening intensified during the early morning, producing numerous tornadoes. A particularly active region, in which there were some strong tornadoes,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-69) was the [Interstate 81](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_81 "Interstate 81") corridor extending from southwest [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"),[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-washingtonpost1-70) northward through the [Shenandoah Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenandoah_Valley "Shenandoah Valley")[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-71) and into [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-72) and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). This included the deadly EF3 tornado that struck the town of [Glade Spring, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glade_Spring,_Virginia "Glade Spring, Virginia"), very early in the morning, where three people died.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-73) Tornadoes were also reported in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"),[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-74)[Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"),[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-75)[North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-76) and [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). Most of these tornadoes were weak. Although tornado watches were issued, no tornadoes were spotted in [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey")[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-77) or [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-washingtonpost1-70) In the wake of the tornadoes and severe thunderstorms, widespread flooding hit the Midwest, South, and Eastern Seaboard, with extensive flood and flash flood warnings issued.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-78) The last tornadoes of the outbreak touched down that afternoon in eastern [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), which was hard hit in the [April 16 outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_14%E2%80%9316,_2011 "Tornado outbreak of April 14–16, 2011"), though the tornadoes that impacted the area this time around were weak.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-79) After spawning one final round of isolated non-tornadic thunderstorms across central Florida that night into April 29, the system finally moved out into the Atlantic Ocean, having caused a great deal of devastation on its 4-day trek throughout the central and eastern US.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-80)

A record 368 tornadoes touched down over the span of four days, 37 of which were EF3+ tornadoes. This section is about the 2011 EF2 tornado. For the tornado that impacted similar areas in 2014, see [2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mayflower%E2%80%93Vilonia_tornado "2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado").

The first tornado of the outbreak to cause more than one death was this long-tracked, high-end EF2 wedge tornado that struck the small town of [Vilonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilonia,_Arkansas "Vilonia, Arkansas") in [Faulkner County, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulkner_County,_Arkansas "Faulkner County, Arkansas"), around 7:30 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (00:30 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")) on April 25.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSLittleRockApril27-83) A [tornado warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") was issued for the area roughly 30 minutes prior to the tornado's arrival, and the relatively low loss of life was attributed to this lead time.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-TheCabin426-84) A [tornado emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") was declared at 7:24 p.m. CDT (00:24 UTC) for the city shortly before the tornado struck.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-85) Four people were killed in the town and many more were injured. The tornado touched down northwest of [Ferndale](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ferndale,_Arkansas&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ferndale, Arkansas (page does not exist)") in [Pulaski County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Arkansas "Pulaski County, Arkansas") at 6:48 p.m. CDT (23:48 UTC), downing trees and transmission towers at EF1 intensity.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-86) It continued northeast of [Natural Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Steps,_Arkansas "Natural Steps, Arkansas"), severely damaging a small church and downing numerous trees, one of which landed on a house.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-87) The tornado continued to knock down trees as it passed near [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland,_Arkansas "Roland, Arkansas"), several of which landed on homes. The tornado reached EF2 strength as it crossed into Faulkner County and passed southeast of [Mayflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower,_Arkansas "Mayflower, Arkansas"), downing numerous trees and power lines and damaging homes and outbuildings. Past Mayflower, it continued towards Vilonia and struck a mobile home park, where numerous mobile homes were destroyed and the four fatalities occurred. Two of the fatalities occurred when a couple attempted to take shelter in a cargo container, which was thrown 150 yards (140 m) and deposited near a pond. Several other people were injured in this area as well. The tornado maintained EF2 intensity as it moved directly through Vilonia, damaging numerous homes and businesses and flipping several semi-trucks. The [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross") indicated that approximately 34 site-built houses and 62 mobile homes were destroyed, 91 site-built homes and 41 mobile homes suffered major damage, 145 site-built houses and 43 mobile homes had minor damage, and 53 site-built houses and 38 mobile homes were affected in some other way in the Vilonia area.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-88) One of the mobile homes was picked up and flipped, and the home's two bathtubs were found over a hill about 40 yards (37 m) away. The lone occupant of the mobile home sustained major injuries.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-89) After moving through Vilonia, the tornado weakened to EF1 strength as it moved into [White County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_County,_Arkansas "White County, Arkansas") and passed west of [El Paso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Arkansas "El Paso, Arkansas"), where trees were blown over onto houses (damaging several roofs), barns and outbuildings were destroyed, an [RV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_vehicle "Recreational vehicle") and the trailer portion of a tractor-trailer were overturned, and hundreds of trees were downed. The tornado finally dissipated north of [Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy,_Arkansas "Joy, Arkansas") at 7:59 p.m. CDT (00:59 UTC), after having travelled just over 51 miles (82 km). At its widest point, the tornado was 1.64 miles (2.64 km) wide.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-TheCabin426-84)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-90) Following the tornado, 85 members of the [U.S. National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_of_the_United_States "National Guard of the United States") were deployed to assist in search and rescue, debris clearing, security and traffic control.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-91)

On April 27, 2014, three years and two days after this tornado, [a violent EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mayflower%E2%80%93Vilonia_tornado "2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado") touched down west of Ferndale and moved along almost the same path as this tornado, causing 16 fatalities and many injuries. However, it affected more of Mayflower than this tornado did and caused greater damage all along the path, especially in Vilonia, before lifting near El Paso.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSLittleRockApril27Vilonia-92)

### Philadelphia–Kemper County, Mississippi

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Philadelphia–Kemper County, Mississippi")]

Philadelphia–Kemper County, Mississippi[![Image 374: A tornado looms over a grassy field near a house, under a gloomy sky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e6/2011_Philadelphia%2C_Mississippi_tornado.png/330px-2011_Philadelphia%2C_Mississippi_tornado.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Philadelphia,_Mississippi_tornado.png)
The tornado in Philadelphia
